opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is that most AI coding tools today are really focused on code *generation*: autocomplete, writing a function, spinning up a new feature. That's valuable, but when you actually go into a large enterprise and watch how engineers spend their time, the majority of it isn't writing new code. It's understanding existing code. It's figuring out why a system was built the way it was, who touched what, what breaks if you change something, and where the tribal knowledge lives.

So Asimov is focused on that comprehension problem first. It's an agent that's meant to deeply understand your entire engineering environment: not just the codebase, but the surrounding context like documentation, chat threads, and the history of decisions that got made along the way. In a big organization, a lot of the most important knowledge was never written down in the code itself. It's in someone's head, or buried in a conversation from two years ago.

Our view is that if you want agents that can eventually do meaningful autonomous work inside an enterprise, they have to understand the system as well as a senior engineer who's been there for years. Generation without understanding gets you a lot of plausible-looking code that doesn't fit the system. So we see Asimov as the foundation layer: get comprehension really right, make engineering teams dramatically faster at onboarding, debugging, and making changes safely, and that becomes the basis for more autonomous capabilities over time.

And practically, for enterprises, that also means taking things like security, deployment flexibility, and working with their actual messy, sprawling codebases seriously, rather than optimizing for a demo on a clean greenfield repo.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts existing tools’ focus on code generation with Asimov’s focus on understanding existing codebases and their surrounding context.

r002.rationale: It says engineers spend most of their time understanding existing code, but does not state that AI coding tools have less impact on enterprise productivity than people expect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about Asimov is that most coding tools today are really focused on the act of writing code, right? Autocomplete, generating a function, maybe fixing a bug. And that's valuable. But if you actually look at how an engineer spends their time inside a large company, writing code is a surprisingly small fraction of it. Most of the time is spent on understanding. Why does this system work the way it does? Who made this decision three years ago and why? What happens if I change this thing over here, what else breaks?

And none of that information lives in the code. It lives in Slack threads, in design docs, in old pull request discussions, in the heads of the two senior engineers who've been there the longest. So when a coding agent only sees the repository, it's working with maybe a third of the context a real engineer has.

So what we're building with Asimov is really a system that ingests all of that, the code, the docs, the conversations, the tickets, and builds a kind of shared memory of the engineering organization. And then the agents operating on top of that can actually reason about the codebase the way a tenured engineer would. We like to say we're building the thing that reads everything so your engineers don't have to.

Where that fits in the landscape, I'd say we're complementary to the code-generation tools. If Copilot or Cursor is the hands, we're trying to be more like the institutional memory. And for enterprises specifically, that turns out to be the bottleneck. Onboarding takes months, knowledge walks out the door when people leave, and every outage comes down to someone not knowing something that somebody else in the company already knew. That's the problem we think is actually worth solving, and frankly it's the one that gets harder, not easier, as organizations scale.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts other tools’ code writing and generation focus with Asimov’s focus on understanding codebases through organizational context and shared memory.

r002.rationale: It says writing code is a small fraction of engineers’ time and describes enterprise knowledge gaps, but does not state that AI coding tools’ impact on enterprise productivity is much lower than expected.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question for enterprises is whether an AI can understand enough of their software to take on meaningful work. Writing code is one part of that. You also need to figure out where a change belongs, what depends on it, and how to verify that it does what you intended.

That’s how I’d frame Asimov’s role: helping move from assistance on an individual coding task toward completing work in the context of a larger codebase. The bar is whether engineers can delegate something useful, understand what came back, and trust it enough to ship.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes understanding and working within a larger codebase, but does not state that existing coding tools primarily focus on code generation or explicitly contrast their focus with Asimov’s.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that AI coding tools’ actual enterprise productivity impact is much lower than expected.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to frame Asimov is: generating code is one part of doing software engineering inside an enterprise. The harder problem is understanding an existing system—why it was built a certain way, what depends on it, and how you know a change is actually correct.

So the role we see for Asimov is to take on more of that complete engineering task. You want to move from a tool that helps you write a function to something you can give a meaningful piece of work, and have it understand the context, make the change, and verify the result.

For enterprises, that distinction matters. Producing more code isn’t necessarily valuable. Reliably getting work done in a codebase people already depend on—that’s the bar.

r001.rationale: It contrasts tools that help write code with Asimov taking on the broader engineering task, especially understanding existing systems and their dependencies.

r002.rationale: It says producing more code is not necessarily valuable and emphasizes reliable work, but does not state that AI coding tools’ enterprise productivity impact is much lower than people expect.
